3rd Battalion, 39th Infantry (Companies I and K): Company I to the heights in the centre, Company K split between the flanks, on the afternoon of the 19th

894th Tank Destroyer Battalion, brought up early on the 20th for a counterattack that never came; with Combat Command B on Djebel el Hamra from the 21st. Its strength is not recorded

units.name: 2nd Battalion, 13th Armored Regiment (with Companies G and I), Combat Command B's tanks, 'in hull defilade astride the enemy's path' on Djebel el Hamra. Howe gives no count; II Corps had 99 medium tanks running on the evening of the 20th
2nd Battalion, 6th Armored Infantry, Combat Command B, on the southern end of Djebel el Hamra; the DAK's envelopment struck it near Bou Chebka pass at daylight on the 22nd

2nd Battalion, Panzer Grenadier Regiment Afrika, Group Menton: a detachment of it reached Hill 1191 after dark on the 19th

The 'nearly two battalions' of infantry Rommel added to Group Menton on the morning of the 20th; they went along the Tébessa road onto Djebel Zebbeus at 1630, and a battalion of them reached Point 732 at 1530 on the 21st
Group Stotten: 1st Battalion, 8th Panzer Regiment, the DAK's tanks. Five were lost in the minefield on the Tébessa road on the 19th; on the 20th they finished Gore Force. Its count is not recorded

The Centauro Division's tank battalion, Italian M14s, which joined the DAK in the night of 19–20 February and pursued five miles down the Tébessa road on the 20th and 'found no one'. Its count is not recorded
5th Bersaglieri Battalion, up from Fériana in the night of 19–20 February; overtaken near Hill 732 by Combat Command B's tanks on the 22nd with the loss of 'many vehicles and supplies'

Kampfgruppe DAK's artillery: the corps guns, dual-purpose 88s and 'a battery of new German rocket projectors', the Nebelwerfer, whose first barrage on American troops opened the 0830 assault on the 20th
The German party that took Hill 974 on Semmama's shoulder about noon on the 19th and 'could not get down its west face'
A mountain company that tried to get round the American right above Hill 812 on the afternoon of the 19th and failed

10th Panzer Division's motorcycle battalion, committed along the Thala road late on the morning of the 20th; in the night its armoured cars and self-propelled guns pushed the British rear guards north and, in the morning fog, knocked out six Crusaders

events.title: Pull a Stonewall Jackson
events.text: Sidi Bou Zid and Sbeïtla have fallen. Kasserine Pass, 'shaped like a crude capital X', is a mile wide at its narrowest between Djebel Semmama and Djebel Chambi, with the Oued el Hatab cut through its floor; beyond it the road forks for Tébessa and for Thala. At eight the evening before, Fredendall telephoned Col. Alexander Stark of the 26th Infantry: 'go to Kasserine right away and pull a Stonewall Jackson.' About 2,000 men hold a line almost three miles long: the 1st Battalion, 26th Infantry astride the Thala road and Company A on Hill 1191, Col. Moore's 19th Combat Engineers from the Hatab across the Tébessa road to Djebel Zebbeus, two batteries of the 33d Field Artillery, a French battery of 75s, the 805th Tank Destroyers and eight tanks of Company I, 13th Armored. Mines lie unburied across the roads. Rommel, who proposed Tébessa, has Comando Supremo's order for Le Kef instead.

events.title: The probe
events.text: At daybreak the 33d Reconnaissance Battalion tries to take the pass by surprise and is 'too small' to do it; Generalmajor Buelowius' Kampfgruppe DAK takes over. At 7:30 Stark reaches the pass and assumes command from Moore. The British 26th Armoured Brigade under Brig. Dunphie, at Thala, passed to II Corps at six.

events.title: Trucks unloading
events.text: At 10:15 'thirty-five to forty truckloads of enemy infantry' are seen unloading south-east of the pass: Group Menton, two battalions of the Panzer Grenadier Regiment Afrika. About noon Germans take Hill 974 on Semmama's shoulder but cannot get down its west face; a little after noon the French see them climbing both sides of the pass, and Stark reports 'the attack was on'. Rommel is at the entrance with Buelowius, still treating Kasserine as a feint and Sbiba as the main effort. In the afternoon the 3rd Battalion, 39th Infantry arrives: Company I to the centre, Company L up to Hill 1191 with Company A.

events.title: The Tébessa road
events.text: 'The enemy's attack was resumed at 1530' along the Tébessa road toward the inner defile under Djebel Zebbeus. Five tanks are lost in the minefield; a mountain company that tries to get round the American right above Hill 812 fails. At dusk the main attack breaks off, with about 100 Americans taken prisoner. Group Stotten's tanks are drawn back to bivouac south-east of Chambi. Late in the afternoon Dunphie inspects the pass, finds it 'unsatisfactory and deteriorating', and is refused leave to commit his brigade; First Army releases only Lt. Col. Gore's small detachment.

events.title: Hill 1191
events.text: After dark a detachment of Menton's 2nd Battalion reaches Hill 1191, 'a hard climb of more than a mile' above the Thala road. Company A, 26th Infantry is cut off on Semmama and its commander briefly captured. At 8:35 Stark asks Fredendall for armour, tank destroyers, infantry, artillery and air. In the night the Centauro tank battalion and the 5th Bersaglieri come up from Fériana, Rommel orders the 10th Panzer Division from Pichon to Kasserine, and Germans who reach Hill 704 at the north-west exit are driven back. Howe says the night 'cannot be clearly reconstructed from the record'; the map's movements in it are inferred.

events.title: Gore Force
events.text: About four Gore Force, eleven tanks, a motor company and a battery from the 26th Armoured Brigade, reaches the north-west corner of the pass. Early in the morning Stark's line on Semmama is enveloped or pierced; the 3rd Battalion, 6th Armored Infantry comes under his command and climbs toward Hill 1191, and the 894th Tank Destroyers move up for a counterattack. At six Rommel's command of the attack group takes effect. Fog and rain lie over the field.

events.title: The barrage
events.text: At 8:30 both battalions of the Panzer Grenadier Regiment Afrika attack with all the DAK's artillery, the dual-purpose 88s and 'a battery of new German rocket projectors': the Nebelwerfer's first barrage on American troops. Late in the morning Rommel, with Buelowius and von Broich, raises Menton's infantry to nearly four battalions and commits the 10th Panzer's motorcycle battalion along the Thala road. Dunphie orders Gore forward about ten (Rickard).

events.title: Moore's command post
events.text: Before noon a German column penetrates between two of Moore's engineer companies and 'Colonel Moore's command post had been overrun'. At noon Kesselring meets Rommel at his advanced post north-west of Kasserine and they agree to break out that day. Early in the afternoon German tanks come through the minefield on the Tébessa road, the 33d Field Artillery is pulled back, the French fire off their last rounds and disable their 75s, and the tank destroyers and then Company I's tanks give way at the inner defile.

events.title: The breakout
events.text: At 4:30 Buelowius' and von Broich's elements attack side by side: the 10th Panzer's armoured infantry on the right over Hill 974 to the valley floor, the DAK along the Tébessa road onto Djebel Zebbeus. The Tébessa road opens first; the Centauro's tanks pursue five miles down it and find no one. Gore Force fights until its last tank is destroyed and its remnant withdraws past Hill 704 at dusk with five of the 805th's destroyers. A platoon of Company I is overrun. The 3rd Battalion, 6th Armored Infantry and parts of the 26th and 39th are cut off on Semmama; through the night their survivors infiltrate west across the Foussana valley or north toward Thala. At seven II Corps counts 99 medium and 47 light tanks running.

events.title: Night on the Thala road
events.text: German armoured cars and self-propelled guns push the British rear guards north along the Thala road in the night. At midnight Robinett and Dunphie confer at Thala: await the attack, counterattack on the outer flanks, conserve tanks. Combat Command B struggles south down the dirt road from Haïdra toward Djebel el Hamra, and the 580th Reconnaissance Battalion comes from the 21st Panzer to hold the pass. Only 'somewhat more than one half' of the 10th Panzer reached Kasserine by nightfall; its heavy battalion with the Tigers stayed with von Arnim.

events.title: Toward Djebel el Hamra
events.text: At two the 33d Reconnaissance Battalion, with a few Italian tanks, leaves the pass north-west along the Tébessa road; about eight miles short of Djebel el Hamra it meets the Reconnaissance Company, 13th Armored, and draws back east. By morning the bulk of Combat Command B is 'along the eastern face of that ridge and in the passes at its center and northern end', the 2nd Battalion, 13th Armored in hull defilade astride the enemy's path, and the pass's stragglers are formed into provisional companies at its foot. Nickforce opens at Thala at six under Brig. Nicholson. At 11:25, told that only small American forces stand east of Hamra, Rommel resumes the offensive on both roads without waiting for air reconnaissance.

events.title: The Thala road
events.text: About 9:30 the 7th Panzer Regiment begins to advance up the Thala road: thirty tanks, twenty self-propelled guns and thirty-five half-track carriers, in fog that has already cost the 17th/21st Lancers six light Crusaders. Dunphie's fifty tanks, 'mostly obsolete Valentines' by Atkinson's count, hold a ridge about nine miles south of Thala until four at the cost of fifteen tanks, then a second line for over an hour, then fall back on the Leicesters.

events.title: Buelowius turns west
events.text: 'General Buelowius' main force left Kasserine pass at 1400' for Djebel el Hamra along the Tébessa road. About 3:30 a battalion of its infantry comes up beside the 33d Reconnaissance near Point 732. At 4:30 the column comes under the fire of Combat Command B's artillery, Stukas strike CCB, and the tanks in hull defilade stop the attack 'about four miles short' of the ridge. About six the DAK pulls back south-east, and Rommel authorises a wide envelopment to the south during the night.

events.title: The Leicesters' ridge
events.text: About seven Dunphie's vehicles pass through the 2nd/5th Leicesters on the last ridge south of Thala, and German tanks follow 'directly after' them; Atkinson has a captured Valentine lead eight panzers through the line. For three hours British tanks, infantry and guns fight the 10th Panzer in the dark among their own positions. 'After three hours, the enemy's offensive was stopped'; the Germans withdraw 1,200 yards with about 700 prisoners, some 300 of them Leicesters. At eight, by Atkinson's account, Brig. Gen. Irwin reaches Thala with the 9th Division's artillery after a march of more than 800 miles in four days.

events.title: Irwin's guns
events.text: In the early hours the 34th Field Artillery's twelve 155s are emplaced along the road west of Thala and the 105s of the 60th and 84th about 3,000 yards south: 48 guns and 2,200 men. Just before dawn Nicholson counterattacks with some of his remaining tanks and loses five or more; von Broich reads it as a major Allied attack and at seven, by Atkinson, telephones Rommel to put off his own. Through the morning Irwin's guns answer the German shelling, and XII Air Support Command flies 114 sorties over Thala in low cloud.

events.title: Bou Chebka
events.text: At daylight the DAK's envelopment strikes the 2nd Battalion, 16th Infantry, the 2nd Battalion, 6th Armored Infantry and the 33d Field Artillery near Bou Chebka pass. Battery C is cut off and loses five howitzers, three 40 mm guns and thirty vehicles. About 9:30 a reconnaissance report misleads Buelowius about what stands in front of him.

events.title: Rommel decides
events.text: In the afternoon Kesselring comes to Rommel's command post and they agree to break off and turn against Montgomery at Mareth; Rommel orders his forces to pass to the defensive (Rickard puts the decision at 2:15). At four Combat Command B counterattacks: the 16th Infantry on the right, the 2nd Battalion, 6th Armored Infantry on the left, Company G of the 13th Armored sortieing. Battery C's eight guns and its vehicles are recovered serviceable, and the 5th Bersaglieri are overtaken near Hill 732 and lose 'many vehicles and supplies'. At 11:10 that night Ambrosio's radio order to retire arrives.

events.title: Back in the pass
events.text: By the forenoon the Axis withdrawal into the pass is complete; the 10th Panzer holds it and the DAK leaves for Fériana in the afternoon, under 'no significant Allied pressure'. Maj. Gen. Harmon arrived in the night to take charge of the front; Nickforce is dissolved at eight that evening. Rommel claims 845 prisoners, 66 tanks, 74 self-propelled guns and reconnaissance vehicles and 48 anti-tank guns for 19–22 February; the German loss table for 16–24 February gives 989 men and 20 tanks. The 1st Battalion, 26th Infantry, the 19th Engineers and the 3rd Battalion, 39th lost 465 men in the pass, most of them missing.

losses: In the pass, 19–20 Feb (Howe): 1st Bn 26th Infantry 6 killed, 35 wounded, 119 missing; 19th Engineers 11, 28, 89; 3rd Bn 39th Infantry 11, 30, 136. Gore Force all eleven tanks. The 26th Armoured Brigade 29 of 50 tanks by midnight on the 21st and five or more at dawn on the 22nd (Atkinson, Howe). The Leicesters about 300 prisoners of some 700 taken at Thala. Battery C, 33d FA five howitzers, three 40 mm guns and thirty vehicles, the guns recovered on the 22nd. The 9th Division Artillery 45 casualties. II Corps for the whole 14–24 Feb: about 300 killed, 3,000 wounded and 3,000 missing, 183 tanks (secondary totals).

16–24 Feb, the German table: 989 men (201 killed, 536 wounded, 252 missing), 20 tanks, 6 armoured vehicles, 61 motor vehicles, 5 anti-tank guns. The 10th Panzer lost nine tanks at Thala (Atkinson); the 5th Bersaglieri 'many vehicles and supplies' near Hill 732. No count for the pass alone.
outcome.note: Rommel claimed 845 prisoners, 66 tanks, 74 self-propelled guns and reconnaissance vehicles, 48 anti-tank guns, 10 guns and 8 aircraft for 19–22 Feb; the 10th Panzer alone 571 prisoners and 38 tanks at Thala. German claims count what was taken, not Allied dead.

sources: George F. Howe, Northwest Africa: Seizing the Initiative in the West (US Army Center of Military History, 1957), chapters XXIII and XXIV: the ground, Stark Force and its reinforcements, Gore Force, the German groups, the clock times, the Thala and Djebel el Hamra fighting, the claims and the loss table for 16–24 February.
Rick Atkinson, An Army at Dawn (2002), the Thala chapter: the 26th Armoured Brigade's tank counts, the Leicesters, Irwin's march and the night of 21–22 February.
J. Rickard, 'Battle of the Kasserine Pass, 19–22 February 1943', historyofwar.org (2017): a few clock times Howe lacks, marked as his.

GLO-30 sampled at 100 m over a 52 km square; it is a surface model, so the modern city of Kasserine and the farms of the Foussana basin show. Roads and the Oued el Hatab from OpenStreetMap; the Tébessa road west of the basin, the track from Haïdra and the Bou Chebka road are drawn from the narrative.

Clock: the times as recorded, read as a GMT+1 clock; sunrise 7:08 and sunset 18:12 are computed for 19 February on that assumption. Fog and rain covered the field on 20 and 21 February and low cloud and showers on the 22nd.

What is reconstructed: the named hills (1191, 974, 712, 704, Zebbeus, Point 732, the Thala ridges, the Hamra passes, Bou Chebka pass), fitted to Howe's prose on the Copernicus DEM within a kilometre or two; every Axis tank and infantry count below the figures Howe gives (30 tanks, 20 self-propelled guns and 35 half-tracks for the 10th Panzer at Thala; eleven tanks for Gore; eight for Company I, 13th Armored); the 19th Engineers', 805th and 894th Tank Destroyers' strengths; the routes between recorded places; and the hours of the night movements of 19–20 and 20–21 February, which Howe says cannot be clearly reconstructed.
